Developments

A development is a cash flow problem before it is a design problem

We work with landowners and developers from the feasibility through to the last unit sold, and we bring the modeling discipline of a financial advisory practice to it.

The problem we are usually brought in to solve

Small and mid-scale Caribbean developments rarely fail on the architecture. They fail on sequencing, on a unit mix nobody tested against who is actually buying, on a price set from what the land cost rather than from what the market will carry, and on a release schedule that puts the whole scheme on the market at once and then discounts it.

Every one of those is a modeling question. The practice behind this firm builds three-year financial models for banks and credit unions. The same discipline, applied to a development, answers what to build, in what order, at what price, and funded how.

What we are asked for most

  • Is this site worth developing, and at what density
  • What mix of units, and how many of each
  • What price will actually clear, by unit type
  • How many phases, and what has to sell before the next one starts
  • What the funding gap is, and when it bites
  • Who buys this, and where do they come from

How we work

Six stages, in sequence

01. Feasibility

Site, title, planning position, utilities and access tested first, because a constraint found in month one is a design decision and a constraint found in month ten is a write-off. Then the development appraisal: land, build, professional fees, finance, marketing and sales costs against a revenue line built bottom-up from comparable evidence.

02. Unit mix and pricing

Who is buying in this market, at what price, and what are they buying. The mix is set from demand evidence rather than from what fits the footprint. Pricing is built per unit type and per floor, with a view on what each premium is worth.

03. Phasing and the funding plan

The cash flow across the whole program, month by month, with the sales required to release each phase. This is where most schemes are won or lost, and it is the piece a financial modeling practice does better than a marketing agency.

04. Release and marketing

A private register ahead of launch, a staged public release, and the collateral the units deserve. We do not launch a whole scheme at once and then discount it.

05. Sales and buyer qualification

Representation through to contract, with buyers qualified for finance before a unit is held rather than after. Where a buyer is coming from abroad, the finance, the landholding position and the currency transfer are dealt with at the start.

06. Completion and handover

Closing coordination with attorneys on both sides, and a handover pack the owner can actually use. Where there is a body corporate, we help set the first-year budget on real numbers rather than optimistic ones.

Properties

What we represent, and what to check before you buy it

Homes, land and commercial property across the Caribbean. Below is what each type actually involves in this region, written plainly, because most of what goes wrong in a Caribbean property purchase goes wrong before the price is ever negotiated.

A note on listings

Where what you see here comes from

We publish property from three places: our own instructions, developments we market under agreement with the developer, and listings shared with us by the agent who holds the instruction. Every listing names which of the three it is, so you always know who we are acting for.

A good deal of the best stock in this region never reaches a public page at all. Owners at this level often prefer it that way, and registered buyers are sent those privately.

Tell us what you are looking for, and we will tell you what exists. Register what you are looking for.

Type 01

Condominiums

A condominium is two purchases in one: the unit, and a share of everything outside its walls. The second is where the cost lives and where the surprises are.

  • The strata or condominium plan, and exactly what your title covers
  • The body corporate budget, the reserve fund, and whether it is actually funded
  • Arrears across the building, because other owners' arrears become your problem
  • Insurance on the common property, and what it excludes in a storm year
  • Bylaws on letting, short-term rental and pets, before you plan on rental income
  • Any special assessment already resolved on or being discussed

Type 02

Townhouses

More space and your own front door, usually at a lower cost per square foot than a comparable detached house, and usually with some shared structure or shared grounds.

  • Whether it is freehold, strata, or freehold with a management company over the grounds
  • Party wall and shared roof responsibilities, in writing
  • Boundaries, parking rights and access, as surveyed rather than as described
  • What the service charge covers, if there is one
  • Resale history in the scheme, which tells you more than any appraisal

Type 03

Villas and estates

The discreet end of the market. Many of the best houses in the region never appear on a public listing, and owners at this level expect their name kept out of it.

  • Represented quietly. Nothing published without the owner's written instruction
  • Title, survey and encroachments checked before a viewing is arranged
  • Water, power and connectivity resilience, which matter more here than anywhere
  • Running cost modeled honestly: staff, maintenance, insurance, standby power
  • Rental potential assessed on evidence, not on what a management company projects

Type 04

Land

The cheapest thing to buy and the easiest thing to get wrong. Most land problems in this region are title problems, access problems or utility problems, and all three are discoverable before you pay.

  • Title and the chain behind it, including family land and undivided interests
  • A current survey, and whether the boundaries on the ground match the plan
  • Legal access, as a registered right rather than a track everyone has always used
  • Water, power and sewerage: whether they reach the parcel and what connection costs
  • Planning and zoning position, and any covenant restricting what can be built
  • Slope, drainage and flood exposure, which decide the real cost of building
  • Where the buyer is not a national, the landholding license position in that market

Type 05

Commercial

A commercial building is an income stream with a roof on it. It is valued on the income and on how safe the income is, which makes the lease and the tenant the asset.

  • The lease: term, rent review, break clauses, and who repairs what
  • The tenant covenant, which is the real security behind the yield
  • Net yield after management, insurance, vacancy and non-recoverable cost
  • Building condition, and the deferred maintenance the vendor has been living with
  • Hurricane insurance terms, deductible and business interruption cover
  • Use class, licensing and parking, before a change of use is assumed

Invest

Buying in the Caribbean from somewhere else

Most of our buyers are not resident in the market they are buying in. That changes the landholding position, the financing, the tax exposure and the way the property has to be run once it is yours.

Start here

Four questions decide whether a Caribbean purchase works for a non-resident buyer, and they are better answered before an offer than after one.

  • Can you hold it, and what license or approval does a non-national need in that market
  • How is it funded, locally or from home, and in which currency
  • What does it actually earn, net of the costs nobody puts in the brochure
  • What happens when you want to sell, and how long does that take here

Where we work

We have advised and operated in Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Curacao, Dominica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Sint Maarten, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. We are building standing in Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, the Turks and Caicos Islands, Barbados, the Cayman Islands and Grenada, which carry much of the premium end of the regional market.

Where our standing in a market is a referral relationship rather than a brokerage, we say so before we act rather than after.

01

Yield and rental analysis

A gross yield quoted off a peak-season nightly rate is not a yield. We model the net, and we model it on evidence.

  • Occupancy modeled by season, not averaged across the year
  • Management, cleaning and platform commission taken out, at real rates
  • Insurance at Caribbean premiums, with the deductible shown separately
  • Maintenance, standby power and a genuine reserve for storm damage
  • Body corporate or service charges, and any letting restriction in the bylaws
  • The result expressed as net yield on total cost, including closing costs

We do not publish indicative yields on this site. A number without the property behind it is marketing, not analysis.

02

Citizenship by investment

Five Eastern Caribbean states operate citizenship by investment programs: Saint Kitts and Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, and Saint Lucia. Real estate is one of the qualifying routes in each, through government-approved projects.

  • Only an approved project qualifies, and the approved list changes
  • Thresholds, fees and holding periods are set by each government and are revised
  • Applications are filed through an authorized agent, not through an estate agency
  • The property decision and the citizenship decision are separate decisions

We will tell you which approved projects exist in a market, introduce you to an authorized agent, and model the investment as a property investment on its own merits. We confirm current thresholds and terms with the relevant authority or authorized agent at the time, because they move, and we will not quote you a figure from memory.

03

Financing and insurance

Property, finance, insurance, conveyancing and currency transfer are five transactions that have to close in order. We coordinate them through licensed partners.

  • Mortgage introduction to regional lenders, with the buyer qualified before a unit is held
  • Insurance arranged through licensed partners, including the hurricane terms
  • Conveyancing by an attorney admitted in the market where the property sits
  • Currency transfer through a licensed provider rather than a retail bank spread

Where a buyer we introduce takes a mortgage, an insurance policy, a conveyancing instruction or a currency transfer through one of these partners, we may be paid an introduction fee by that partner. We tell you before the introduction, every time, and you are never obliged to use anyone we suggest. The full position is on one page.

How we are paid

Every way this firm earns money, on one page

We would rather you learned this from us than worked it out later. Nothing below is unusual in the industry. What is unusual is publishing it.

The principle

Each part of the house says how it is paid

St. Jean & Co. Real Estate sits beside an advisory practice, a markets platform and a technology business. Rather than defend one blanket claim of independence across all of them, we hold them apart by rule and make each one state its own economics. This page is this firm's statement.

The three ways

What we earn, and who pays it

SourceWho paysHow it works
Sales and letting commissionThe seller or the landlord Agreed in writing, as a percentage or a fixed fee, before we act on an instruction. A buyer does not pay us a commission on a purchase.
Advisory and development feesThe client who engages us Feasibility, appraisal, unit mix, pricing and release strategy, charged as a fixed fee for a defined scope. Not contingent on a sale, so the advice is not bent toward one.
Introduction fees from partnersThe lender, insurer, attorney or transfer provider Where a client we introduce proceeds with a licensed partner, that partner may pay us an introduction fee. It is paid by them, not added to your cost by us.

Rates are set per instruction and per market. We quote them in writing before an engagement starts, and we do not publish a schedule here because a number without the instruction behind it would mislead.

The third one, in full

The rules we put around introduction fees

We tell you first

Before we introduce you to a lender, an insurer, an attorney or a currency transfer provider, we tell you in writing that we may be paid for the introduction, and by whom. Before, not in the small print afterward.

You are never obliged

You can use your own lender, your own attorney, your own insurer and your own bank. The instruction is not conditional on using anyone we suggest, and the price of the property does not change either way.

We say when a cheaper route exists

If a partner who pays us is not the best answer for you, we will say so. The introduction fee is not large enough to be worth our reputation, and we would rather you came back.

We tell you the amount if you ask

Ask what we are being paid on your transaction and we will tell you the figure. No client has to work it out.

Why we kept this revenue rather than dropping it: we are a boutique, the work has to pay for itself, and a firm that quietly forgoes a fee is no more honest than one that discloses it. The answer that survives scrutiny is to take it, disclose it, and bind ourselves on how it is handled.

What we will not do

Four things, so you can hold us to them

  • We do not take a fee from both sides of the same sale without telling both sides in writing
  • Every property we publish is here under our own instruction, a co-broke agreement with the listing agent, or a marketing agreement with the developer, and the listing says which
  • We do not quote a yield, a price or a threshold we cannot source
  • We do not invent testimonials, case studies or transaction counts, here or anywhere

The advisory practice

St. Jean & Company is a separate unit with its own rule

The advisory practice does not trade, lend or underwrite, holds no balance sheet, and is never paid for placing an instrument on the other side of its own advice. It is a different business with a different economics statement, and the two are held apart deliberately. stjeanco.com.

About

The property arm of an advisory practice

St. Jean & Co. Real Estate represents homes, land and developments across the Caribbean. It is the property arm of St. Jean & Company, a strategic and financial advisory firm registered in Nevis.

What that actually means for you

An estate agency sells. An advisory practice is paid to tell a board the thing it does not want to hear. This firm was built out of the second, and it shows in what we do before a property is ever marketed: the title is checked, the numbers are modeled, and if the price is wrong we say so at the start.

It also means the analysis behind a development appraisal or a rental model is the same analysis the practice runs for banks and credit unions. That is an unusual thing to find behind a property listing in this region, and it is the whole reason this arm exists.

Where we work

The firm has advised and operated in Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Curacao, Dominica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Sint Maarten, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Those are markets we have worked in rather than markets we have read about, and they are where this arm starts.

They are not where it stops. A great deal of the premium end of Caribbean property sits in Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, the Turks and Caicos Islands, Barbados, the Cayman Islands and Grenada. We are building standing in those markets, and we take instructions there as the agreements and the licensing allow.

The right to earn a commission is set market by market. In some of them a firm registered elsewhere may refer a buyer but may not broker, and The Bahamas is one. We tell you which position applies to your market before we act, and we do not present a referral as a representation.

Your position

The facility

Debt service ratios, loan to value limits and rates differ by lender and by market, and a non-resident borrower is usually held to tighter terms than a resident. This tells you the shape of what is possible. EZirates confirms what a lender will actually do.

Get pre-qualified through EZirates

Tool 03 Powered by EZirates

Insurance cost estimator

Property insurance in this region is priced on hazard, not on postcode. Here is what drives it and what it comes to.

The risk

What moves the rate

  • Construction. Reinforced concrete rates well below timber frame
  • Roof. Material, pitch, age and whether it is strapped or bolted
  • Coastal proximity and elevation, which drive both wind and surge
  • Flood zone and drainage on the parcel
  • The windstorm deductible you accept. Taking more cuts the premium
  • Claims history on the property and in the area
  • Whether cover is written locally or placed with a reinsurer
  • Occupancy. A let property is not rated as an owner-occupied one
The rate per hundred is the one number you cannot guess. It is set by the underwriter on the specifics above. Enter a rate to model the cost, then let EZirates obtain the real one.

Request a quotation through EZirates

Tool 04

Cost to close

The price is not the cost. This is the cash you need on top of it, and for a non-national buyer it is usually larger than expected.

The Firm

Sustainability

In this region sustainability is not a brochure word. It is whether the building is still standing in October.

A Caribbean property that cannot survive a storm season, a drought or a grid failure is not a sustainable asset. It is a liability with a view.

Resilience

Roof fixing, structural tie-down, impact glazing and setback are the four things that decide whether a property is insurable at a sensible premium. We look at them on every instruction and we tell you what we find.

There is a direct financial consequence. A building that underwrites well costs less to insure every year it stands, and the insurance line is usually the second largest running cost after finance.

Water and energy

Catchment and cistern capacity, solar generation and battery storage, and whether the property can run through a grid outage. On many islands these are not improvements, they are the difference between a house you can use and one you cannot.

On our own developments

Where we develop, we build to the resilience standard we would want our own insurer to see, and we publish what we specified. A developer who will not tell you how the roof is fixed is telling you something.

What we check

Six questions on every property we represent

01How the roof is fixed to the structure, and when it was last inspected
02Glazing specification, and whether openings are protected
03Elevation, setback and surface water drainage on the parcel
04Water catchment and storage capacity in days of normal use
05Generation and storage, and how long the property runs without the grid
06The insurance history, and what the underwriter asked for last time

Investing with us

We acquire and develop on our own account, alongside the brokerage. This page says how that works and where the line sits.

Most agencies sell you property. We also buy it, which means our analysis has to survive our own money.

What we do

St. Jean & Co. Real Estate acquires and develops residential property in the Eastern Caribbean, beginning with our own four-home scheme on St. Kitts. We take positions where the modeling supports it and we hold through delivery rather than flipping entitlements.

Why it matters to a buyer

A firm that only brokers learns the market second hand. A firm that also builds knows what a roof costs this quarter, what the utility connection actually takes, and which contractor finishes. That knowledge goes into every appraisal we give you.

And the line

Where we hold an interest in a property we are showing you, we say so on the listing, in writing, before you view it. We never present our own stock as though it were a neutral recommendation. The full economics are on one page.

Acquisitions

What we are looking to buy, stated plainly, so that an owner or an agent knows in one minute whether to call.

We would rather publish the brief than waste an owner's afternoon.

Markets

Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Sint Maarten and Curacao as the priority. Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines considered on the right asset.

What we buy

Development land with services at or near the boundary and a planning position we can resolve. Part-built or stalled schemes where the problem is capital or sequencing rather than design. Income-producing residential blocks. Commercial with a tenant and a lease we can underwrite.

What we will not buy

Anything with unresolved title, undivided family interests, or access that exists by custom rather than by right. Anything where the flood or surge exposure cannot be insured at a sensible premium. We walk away from those rather than price them.

We publish a regional financial title. The property reporting comes from the same desk.

The Caribbean Ledger

St. Jean & Company publishes The Caribbean Ledger, a pan-Caribbean financial title with a business and policy desk. Interest rates, construction cost, insurance capacity, planning reform and the citizenship programmes all move property values in this region, and all of them are covered there.

Property market notes will be published here and linked from the Ledger as they are written.

Why this page is empty

Most firms fill this section the week they launch, with work done elsewhere, by other people, under other names. We would rather you found this page empty and knew that when something appears on it, it is ours and the client agreed to it being here.

The first case study will be the development currently in progress, published when it completes.
